title: Multi-particle gates on driven one-dimensional paths: probing deep traps
authors: Harsh Jain, Shankar Ghosh, Archishman Raju
abstract: We study single-file transport of driven overdamped colloidal particles on a periodic path with deep potential wells. In the small trap limit (i.e., trap size smaller than particle size), the particle current transitions from zero to finite as the number of particles on the path exceeds a critical number $n_c$. Beyond this threshold, $n_c$ particles cluster behind the trap, demonstrating collective correlated motion. The remaining `extra' particles circulate, giving a finite current. We study this phenomenon numerically using overdamped Brownian dynamics simulations, and present an experimental realization of this behaviour for micron-scale colloidal particles driven in an optical vortex. Using our experimental observations, we present results characterizing potential wells as deep as several hundred $k_BT$.
summary: The research explores how interacting colloidal particles exhibit collective motion when driven through deep potential traps, mimicking particle-gate physics. By combining Brownian dynamics simulations with optical trapping experiments, the authors demonstrate a sharp transition to finite current only above a critical particle number ($n_c$). This technique allows for the study of highly confined, non-equilibrium transport regimes relevant to molecular or biological systems.
main_problem: The study investigates single-file transport of colloidal particles driven through periodic potential wells, focusing on how particle interactions induce collective correlated motion.
main_result: A finite current only appears when the number of particles exceeds a critical threshold ($n_c$), demonstrating a particle-gate-like behavior in deep traps. The technique allows characterizing trap depths inaccessible by standard theoretical methods.
method: The work combines overdamped Brownian dynamics simulations with experimental realization using colloidal particles driven by an optical vortex generated via an SLM.
model_or_system: The system models colloidal particles moving on a periodic path under a tilted potential, which is realized experimentally using repulsive electrical double-layer interactions and optically induced driving forces. The theoretical framework involves the overdamped Langevin equation.
key_observables: Particle current ($\langle\gamma_\muangle$), critical cluster size ($n_c$), and particle position shift ($s$).
important_parameters: Trap depth (up to several hundred $k_B T$), force ratio ($f/f_c$), and particle number ($n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the small trap limit ($\alpha L \le 2a$) for certain approximations, and the experimental setup models interactions using DLVO potentials.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate potential well geometries, phase diagrams showing current dependence on $n$ and force ratio, and details of the optical vortex generation setup.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from theoretical modeling of particle-gate behavior in deep traps to detailed experimental implementation using colloidal particles trapped by an optical vortex generated via SLM modulation.
why_interesting: This work provides a physical platform to study non-equilibrium transport and correlated dynamics, which has analogies in open quantum systems where environmental coupling dictates collective behavior.
